# APPROACH TO BACTEREMIA

Bacteremia usually results from a focal infection somewhere in the body. If a focal infection is not obvious, a careful search should be made beginning with a detailed history and physical examination.

If a focal infection seems to be the source of the bacteremia, select antimicrobials active against pathogens likely to be present in the focal infection. Return to the main menu and select the relevant diagnosis or syndrome.

# For infections with signs and/or symptoms of severe sepsis, like hypotension or end organ dysfunction

[Sepsis, severe sepsis, and septic shock](sepsis-and-shock)

# Sequence of evaluation

Obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics when signs or symptoms suggest bacteremia. Obtain 2 or 3 blood culture sets from different venipuncture sites within a 24 hour period. When suspicion is strong and the patient's signs and symptoms have not responded, obtain 2 blood culture sets the next day. For more information about blood cultures, see recommendations on the Q-drive Q:\MICROBIOL INFO FOR CLINICIANS\BLOOD CULTURE Recommendations.doc

# Empirical treatment of suspected bacteremia if local infection is not apparent and blood cultures are not yet positive

[Suspected bacteremia, blood cultures not yet positive](suspected-bacteremia-cultures-not-yet-positive)

Cultures usually become positive after 1 or more days. Usually interim results are reported first, followed by final identification and sensitivities after another day or two. Adjust antimicrobials as appropriate as this sequence unfolds.

# Preliminary results of a positive culture are available

When a focal infection is not apparent, the type of bacteria growing in blood culture might suggest a focal infection and direct the search for a diagnosis.

When a focal infection is apparent, it may suggest the identity of the bacteria growing in blood cultures before the laboratory completes its identification.

Preliminary positive results should lead to changes in antimicrobial therapy to target suspected pathogens, narrow the spectrum, reduce toxicity, and reduce costs.
